claims.text: High-temperature yield-strength retention in the target refractory HEAs is primarily controlled by a temperature-induced transition from screw- to edge-dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Thermoelastic behavior in the target refractory HEAs is primarily controlled by the proposed dislocation-character transition.
NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 sheet material can be fabricated by cold rolling followed by annealing.
The cited NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 material is a single-phase BCC alloy.
Room-temperature deformation in the target alloys is dominated by screw dislocations.
At high temperatures, deformation in the target alloys becomes dominated by edge dislocations.
Rising temperature reduces the glide barrier for edge dislocations.
Chemical disorder in refractory HEAs affects the relative activation and mobility of edge and screw dislocations.
A transition toward edge-dislocation-mediated deformation enhances plastic flow.
Edge-dislocation-mediated deformation supports high-temperature strength retention despite other softening mechanisms.
The dislocation-character transition influences thermoelastic response.
Elevated-temperature microstructures will contain a greater prevalence of edge dislocations that correlates with retained yield strength.
The elevated-temperature specimens will exhibit a modified thermoelastic response relative to the room-temperature baseline.
Room-temperature screw-dominated behavior is typically associated with lower ductility.
Solid-solution strengthening and dynamic recrystallization can contribute to the mechanical response of refractory HEAs at elevated temperature.
Alloying adjustments that alter stacking-fault energy can suppress edge-dislocation formation in the target BCC refractory HEAs.
Combined neutron diffraction and high-resolution TEM can identify the dislocation character associated with strength in BCC refractory HEAs.
